items.readable_text:
Content:
A right conical frustum is the part of a right cone that remains after it is cut by a plane parallel to its base and the top part is removed.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/62f30142b1f660de906366c2899ad9a9]

Content:
A conical frustum is also referred to as a truncated cone.

Content:
We can find the volume of a (right) conical frustum using the formula

Content:
[MATH: V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi h (R^2 + r^2 + R r),]

Content:
where [MATH: r] and [MATH: R] are the radii of the top and bottom bases, respectively, and [MATH: h] is the height of the frustum.

Content:
For example, if

Content:
[MATH: r = 2 \: \textrm{cm}, \qquad R = 5\: \textrm{cm}, \qquad h = 4\: \textrm{cm}]

Content:
then, by substituting these values into the formula, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: V|= (π)/(3)h(R^{2} + r^{2} + R ⋅ r); = (π)/(3)(4)(5^{2} + 2^{2} + 5 ⋅ 2); = (π)/(3) ⋅ 4 ⋅ 39; = 52πcm^{3}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We can find the volume of a conical frustum using the formula

[MATH: V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi h (R^2 + r^2 + R r),]

where [MATH: r] and [MATH: R] are the radii of the bases, and [MATH: h] is the height of the frustum.

Substituting

[MATH: r = 2 \: \textrm{in}, \qquad R = 3 \: \textrm{in}, \qquad h = 4 \: \textrm{in}]

into the formula, we obtain

[MATH: V|= (π)/(3)(4)(3^{2} + 2^{2} + 3 ⋅ 2); = (π)/(3)(4)(19); = (76π)/(3)in^{3}.]

sections.normalized_html: Find the lateral surface area of the conical frustum above.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We can find the lateral surface area of a conical frustum using the formula

[MATH: S_L = \pi(R + r)l,]

where [MATH: r] and [MATH: R] are the radii of the bases, and [MATH: l] is the slant height of the frustum.

First, we will find the slant height of the frustum using the Pythagorean theorem in the right triangle shown above:

[MATH: l|= sqrt((R − r)^{2} + h^{2}); = sqrt((15 − 7)^{2} + 15^{2}); = sqrt(289); = 17in.]

Now, substituting

[MATH: r = 7\: \textrm{in}, \qquad R = 15\: \textrm{in}, \qquad l = 17 \: \textrm{in}]

into the slant height formula, we obtain

[MATH: S_{L}|= π(R + r)l; = π(15 + 7)(17); = 374πin^{2}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We can find the surface area of a conical frustum using the formula

[MATH: S = \pi \big[ (R+r)l + R^2 + r^2 \big],]

where [MATH: r] and [MATH: R] are the radii of the bases, and [MATH: l] is the slant height of the frustum.

First, we will find the slant height of the frustum using the Pythagorean theorem in the right triangle shown above:

[MATH: l|= sqrt((R − r)^{2} + h^{2}); = sqrt((10 − 4)^{2} + (8)^{2}); = sqrt(36 + 64); = sqrt(100); = 10cm.]

Now, substituting

[MATH: r = 4 \: \textrm{cm}, \qquad R = 10 \: \textrm{cm}, \qquad l = 10 \: \textrm{cm}]

into the formula, we obtain

[MATH: S|= π[(10 + 4)(10) + (10)^{2} + (4)^{2}]; = π[140 + 100 + 16]; = 256πcm^{2}.]

Content:
To derive a formula for a conical frustum's volume, we first extend the frustum to form a complete cone.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/71bd0682554cf6f326786d97a0672258]

Content:
Our frustum is the object that remains when we remove the smaller cone (on top) from the larger cone.

Content:
To calculate the volume of the frustum, we subtract the volume of the smaller cone from the volume of the larger cone. This gives

Content:
[MATH: V_{L}|= V_{big} − V_{small}; = (1)/(3)πR^{2}(h + h^{′}) − (1)/(3)πr^{2}h^{′}; = (1)/(3)π(R^{2}h + R^{2}h^{′} − r^{2}h^{′}); = (1)/(3)π(R^{2}h + h^{′}(R^{2} − r^{2})).]

Content:
Now consider the right triangle made by the complete cone, shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/08d5f749ff7a19bf5c15de0aff43bc5d]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \triangle OPT] and [MATH: \triangle OQS] are similar by the AA criterion. So, we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{h'}{r} = \dfrac{h+h'}{R},]

Content:
which can be rewritten as

Content:
[MATH: h^{′}R|= (h + h^{′})r; h^{′}R|= hr + h^{′}r; h^{′}R − h^{′}r|= hr; h^{′}(R − r)|= hr; h^{′}|= (hr)/(R − r).]

Content:
Therefore, the volume of our frustum is

Content:
[MATH: V_{L}|= (1)/(3)π(R^{2}h + h^{′}(R^{2} − r^{2})); = (1)/(3)π(R^{2}h + (hr)/(R − r)(R^{2} − r^{2})); = (1)/(3)π(R^{2}h + (hr)/(R − r)(R − r)(R + r)); = (1)/(3)π(R^{2}h + hr(R + r)); = (1)/(3)πh(R^{2} + rR + r^{2}); = (1)/(3)πh(R^{2} + r^{2} + Rr).]

items.readable_text:
Content:
To derive a formula for a conical frustum's lateral surface area, we first extend the frustum to form a complete cone.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/58fe63d7d8cd135eede00c519a0ca1ff]

Content:
Our frustum is the object that remains when we remove the smaller cone (on top) from the larger cone.

Content:
To calculate the lateral surface area of the frustum, we subtract the lateral surface area of the smaller cone from the larger cone. This gives

Content:
[MATH: S_{L}|= S_{big} − S_{small}; = πR(l + l^{′}) − πrl^{′}; = πl^{′}(R − r) + πlR.]

Content:
Now consider the right triangle made by the complete cone, shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3effd4fc70fdc0ae3cd14e479dbcee3d]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \triangle OPT] and [MATH: \triangle OQS] are similar by the AA criterion. So, we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{r}{l'} = \dfrac{R}{l+l'},]

Content:
which can be rewritten as

Content:
[MATH: Rl^{′}|= r(l + l^{′}); Rl^{′}|= rl + rl^{′}; Rl^{′} − rl^{′}|= rl; l^{′}(R − r)|= rl.]

Content:
Therefore, the lateral surface area of our frustum is

Content:
[MATH: S_{L}|= πl^{′}(R − r) + πlR; = πrl + πRl; = π(r + R)l.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A right conical frustum is the part of a right cone that remains after it is cut by a plane parallel to its base and the top part is removed.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/62f30142b1f660de906366c2899ad9a9]

Content:
A conical frustum is also referred to as a truncated cone.

Content:
We can find the volume of a (right) conical frustum using the formula

Content:
[MATH: V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi h (R^2 + r^2 + R r),]

Content:
where [MATH: r] and [MATH: R] are the radii of the top and bottom bases, respectively, and [MATH: h] is the height of the frustum.

Content:
For example, if

Content:
[MATH: r = 2 \: \textrm{cm}, \qquad R = 5\: \textrm{cm}, \qquad h = 4\: \textrm{cm}]

Content:
then, by substituting these values into the formula, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: V|= (π)/(3)h(R^{2} + r^{2} + R ⋅ r); = (π)/(3)(4)(5^{2} + 2^{2} + 5 ⋅ 2); = (π)/(3) ⋅ 4 ⋅ 39; = 52πcm^{3}.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Volume of a Conical Frustum

Example Prompt:
Determine the volume of the conical frustum below.

[IMG: /graphics/260e130be9b4aa4cc3250282e182ce77]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We can find the volume of a conical frustum using the formula

[MATH: V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi h (R^2 + r^2 + R r),]

where [MATH: r] and [MATH: R] are the radii of the bases, and [MATH: h] is the height of the frustum.

Substituting

[MATH: r = 2 \: \textrm{in}, \qquad R = 3 \: \textrm{in}, \qquad h = 4 \: \textrm{in}]

into the formula, we obtain

[MATH: V|= (π)/(3)(4)(3^{2} + 2^{2} + 3 ⋅ 2); = (π)/(3)(4)(19); = (76π)/(3)in^{3}.]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Lateral Surface Area of a Conical Frustum

Content:
A frustum's lateral surface area is the surface area that does not include the area of the bases.

Content:
Suppose we want to calculate the lateral surface area of the frustum shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ff68ab9af35164b2759e8e7c5178c5fe]

Content:
We can show that the frustum's lateral surface area [MATH: S_L] is given by

Content:
[MATH: S_L = \pi(R + r)l]

Content:
where [MATH: r] and [MATH: R] are the upper and lower radii, respectively, and [MATH: l] is the frustum's slant height.

Content:
We can visualize the net of this lateral surface by imagining that we cut the frustum along one of the slight heights and "unfold" the lateral part.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/29a7dc0635727a6302db0c8bfca69417]

Content:
Doing this, we get the following net.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6273e6ae5baf74a213648e451b34e3e6]

Item 6 — Example: Finding the Lateral Surface Area of a Conical Frustum

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/583b5801e5eacf5ba2f98d1c59b8a835]

Find the lateral surface area of the conical frustum above.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We can find the lateral surface area of a conical frustum using the formula

[MATH: S_L = \pi(R + r)l,]

where [MATH: r] and [MATH: R] are the radii of the bases, and [MATH: l] is the slant height of the frustum.

[IMG: /graphics/c0a3f237c70dc58127822f4201eb0ab2]

First, we will find the slant height of the frustum using the Pythagorean theorem in the right triangle shown above:

[MATH: l|= sqrt((R − r)^{2} + h^{2}); = sqrt((15 − 7)^{2} + 15^{2}); = sqrt(289); = 17in.]

Now, substituting

[MATH: r = 7\: \textrm{in}, \qquad R = 15\: \textrm{in}, \qquad l = 17 \: \textrm{in}]

into the slant height formula, we obtain

[MATH: S_{L}|= π(R + r)l; = π(15 + 7)(17); = 374πin^{2}.]

Item 9 — Tutorial: The Surface Area of a Conical Frustum

Content:
Finally, let's consider the conical frustum below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3c5bca0173dfa61e13ff74097a2048c1]

Content:
The total surface of a right conical frustum is composed of the curved lateral surface and the two circular bases. Therefore, we can calculate the total surface area [MATH: S] of the conical frustum as

Content:
[MATH: S|= S_{L} + S_{T} + S_{B}; = π(R + r)l + πR^{2} + πr^{2}; = π[(R + r)l + R^{2} + r^{2}].]

Content:
where [MATH: r] and [MATH: R] are the radii of the bases, and [MATH: l] is the slant height of the frustum.

---

Item 10 — Example: Finding the Surface Area of a Conical Frustum

Example Prompt:
Find the surface area of the conical frustum below.

[IMG: /graphics/35c1eed6f8898489a81ef764c9da0325]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We can find the surface area of a conical frustum using the formula

[MATH: S = \pi \big[ (R+r)l + R^2 + r^2 \big],]

where [MATH: r] and [MATH: R] are the radii of the bases, and [MATH: l] is the slant height of the frustum.

[IMG: /graphics/292bebd6c0f8e3adda1279b9ef27fae6]

First, we will find the slant height of the frustum using the Pythagorean theorem in the right triangle shown above:

[MATH: l|= sqrt((R − r)^{2} + h^{2}); = sqrt((10 − 4)^{2} + (8)^{2}); = sqrt(36 + 64); = sqrt(100); = 10cm.]

Now, substituting

[MATH: r = 4 \: \textrm{cm}, \qquad R = 10 \: \textrm{cm}, \qquad l = 10 \: \textrm{cm}]

into the formula, we obtain

[MATH: S|= π[(10 + 4)(10) + (10)^{2} + (4)^{2}]; = π[140 + 100 + 16]; = 256πcm^{2}.]

Item 13 — Tutorial: Proof of the Volume Formula

Content:
To derive a formula for a conical frustum's volume, we first extend the frustum to form a complete cone.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/71bd0682554cf6f326786d97a0672258]

Content:
Our frustum is the object that remains when we remove the smaller cone (on top) from the larger cone.

Content:
To calculate the volume of the frustum, we subtract the volume of the smaller cone from the volume of the larger cone. This gives

Content:
[MATH: V_{L}|= V_{big} − V_{small}; = (1)/(3)πR^{2}(h + h^{′}) − (1)/(3)πr^{2}h^{′}; = (1)/(3)π(R^{2}h + R^{2}h^{′} − r^{2}h^{′}); = (1)/(3)π(R^{2}h + h^{′}(R^{2} − r^{2})).]

Content:
Now consider the right triangle made by the complete cone, shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/08d5f749ff7a19bf5c15de0aff43bc5d]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \triangle OPT] and [MATH: \triangle OQS] are similar by the AA criterion. So, we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{h'}{r} = \dfrac{h+h'}{R},]

Content:
which can be rewritten as

Content:
[MATH: h^{′}R|= (h + h^{′})r; h^{′}R|= hr + h^{′}r; h^{′}R − h^{′}r|= hr; h^{′}(R − r)|= hr; h^{′}|= (hr)/(R − r).]

Content:
Therefore, the volume of our frustum is

Content:
[MATH: V_{L}|= (1)/(3)π(R^{2}h + h^{′}(R^{2} − r^{2})); = (1)/(3)π(R^{2}h + (hr)/(R − r)(R^{2} − r^{2})); = (1)/(3)π(R^{2}h + (hr)/(R − r)(R − r)(R + r)); = (1)/(3)π(R^{2}h + hr(R + r)); = (1)/(3)πh(R^{2} + rR + r^{2}); = (1)/(3)πh(R^{2} + r^{2} + Rr).]

---

Item 14 — Tutorial: Proof of the Lateral Surface Area Formula

Content:
To derive a formula for a conical frustum's lateral surface area, we first extend the frustum to form a complete cone.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/58fe63d7d8cd135eede00c519a0ca1ff]

Content:
Our frustum is the object that remains when we remove the smaller cone (on top) from the larger cone.

Content:
To calculate the lateral surface area of the frustum, we subtract the lateral surface area of the smaller cone from the larger cone. This gives

Content:
[MATH: S_{L}|= S_{big} − S_{small}; = πR(l + l^{′}) − πrl^{′}; = πl^{′}(R − r) + πlR.]

Content:
Now consider the right triangle made by the complete cone, shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3effd4fc70fdc0ae3cd14e479dbcee3d]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \triangle OPT] and [MATH: \triangle OQS] are similar by the AA criterion. So, we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{r}{l'} = \dfrac{R}{l+l'},]

Content:
which can be rewritten as

Content:
[MATH: Rl^{′}|= r(l + l^{′}); Rl^{′}|= rl + rl^{′}; Rl^{′} − rl^{′}|= rl; l^{′}(R − r)|= rl.]

Content:
Therefore, the lateral surface area of our frustum is

Content:
[MATH: S_{L}|= πl^{′}(R − r) + πlR; = πrl + πRl; = π(r + R)l.]
